issues.legal_issue: The State must constitute a management committee for a public trust once the statutory chapter governing such trusts applies and the appointed date is fixed.
material_facts: The temple was a public trust whose properties had vested in the State and whose management was controlled by the State’s Devasthan Department.
The State published notifications listing the temple among trusts to which the statutory chapter applied.
The State argued that constituting a management committee was discretionary, while the High Court had directed it to constitute one.
issues.conclusion: Constitution of a management committee is mandatory, not discretionary, once the chapter applies and the relevant appointed date is fixed. The High Court Division Bench’s modifications were set aside and the Single Judge’s judgment was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 52 and 53 of the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, 1959 provide for the chapter’s application to specified public trusts and for management to vest in a committee from an appointed date. The word “shall” ordinarily has imperative force; even a discretionary word may impose a duty when a public power is coupled with an obligation. The Court relied on Commissioner of Police, Bombay v. Gordhandas Bhanji, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Jogendra Singh, State (Delhi Administration) v. I.K. Nangia, Julius v. Lord Bishop of Oxford, and the principle discussed in Maxwell on Interpretation of Statutes. It also referred to N.C. Dhoundial v. Union of India on considering a marginal note in construing a provision.

rule.if: public_trust_management_proceeding and trust_in_covered_class and chapter_coverage_published and appointed_date_fixed

predicates.public_trust_management_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the management of a public trust.
predicates.trust_in_covered_class: The trust belongs to a class of public trusts covered by the statutory management scheme.
predicates.chapter_coverage_published: The government has published a list identifying the trust as covered by the management scheme.
predicates.appointed_date_fixed: The government has fixed the date from which the scheme transfers management to a committee.

issues.definition: When a public-trust management proceeding concerns a covered trust whose coverage has been published and whose appointed date has been fixed, the management committee must be constituted.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory commissioner does not, merely by being an officer subject to State control, constitute a State agency that exempts a public trust from the statutory management scheme.
material_facts: The State argued that the Devasthan Commissioner’s management of the temple brought it within the exemption for trusts administered by an agency under State control.

The Commissioner was a statutory authority and State officer with duties under the Act, but the Act did not provide that the Commissioner could be placed in charge of managing trusts covered by the chapter.
The State had published notifications applying the chapter to the temple.
issues.conclusion: The Devasthan Commissioner was not an agency of the State for the asserted exemption, and the exemption did not remove the temple from the chapter’s application.
issues.legal_principle: Section 77(1) exempts a trust administered by an agency acting under State control or by a local authority. Sections 7, 52 and 53 must be read harmoniously, and the exemption must be construed in the context of the statutory scheme. A statutory authority cannot act outside the statute, and statutory control over an authority does not by itself create a separate State agency. The Court relied on Taylor v. Taylor; Ashok Lanka v. Rishi Dixit and M.P. Gopalakrishnan Nair v. State of Kerala on avoiding absurdity; Reserve Bank of India v. Peerless General Finance and Investment Co. Ltd. on reading a statute as a whole; and Bombay Dyeing and Secretary, Department of Excise & Commercial Taxes v. Sun Bright Marketing (P) Ltd. on harmonious construction.

predicates.public_trust_exemption_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a public trust is exempt from a statutory management scheme.
predicates.trust_managed_by_statutory_officer: A statutory officer manages or supervises the trust and is subject to government control.
predicates.statute_does_not_authorize_officer_to_ma: The governing law does not authorize the statutory officer to manage trusts assigned to the statutory committee scheme.

issues.definition: When an exemption proceeding concerns a trust managed by a government-controlled statutory officer and the law does not authorize that officer to manage trusts covered by the committee scheme, the officer’s management does not exempt the trust as a State agency.

issues.legal_issue: The State may not take a position inconsistent with its prior representations and conduct after inducing others to rely on the position that it would apply the statutory management scheme.
material_facts: In earlier proceedings, the State had stated that it was ready and willing to perform its obligations under the statutory chapter and appoint a committee.
The State issued notifications listing the temple under the chapter after court directions.
The State later argued that the chapter did not apply because the Devasthan Commissioner managed the temple.
issues.conclusion: The State could not be permitted to take the inconsistent position that the chapter did not apply after representing that it would act under the chapter and issuing the notifications.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied estoppel by conduct and acquiescence and the rule against approbating and reprobating. It relied on Karamshi Jethabhai Somayya v. State of Bombay, Cooke v. Rickman, Humphries v. Humphries, and Jai Narain Parasrampura v. Pushpa Devi Saraf, including the principle that a party may be prevented from denying an expectation it knowingly or unknowingly encouraged when denial would be unconscionable.

predicates.public_trust_management_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether the government must act under a statutory public-trust management scheme.
predicates.government_represented_compliance: The government represented that it would perform its obligations under the management scheme.
predicates.government_acted_consistently_with_repre: The government took steps consistent with its representation, such as publishing a list or notifying coverage under the scheme.
predicates.government_later_took_inconsistent_posit: The government later asserted that the scheme did not apply or that it had no corresponding obligation.

issues.definition: When, in a public-trust management proceeding, the government represented compliance, acted consistently with that representation, and later took an inconsistent position, it is precluded from taking that position.

issues.legal_issue: A previously adjudicated determination that a temple is a Jain temple cannot be reopened in later proceedings between the relevant parties.
material_facts: In an earlier round of litigation, the Supreme Court had determined that the temple was a Jain temple, not a Hindu temple.
In the present proceedings, the State and other respondents again sought to contend that it was a Hindu temple.
issues.conclusion: The prior determination that the temple was a Jain temple was binding, and the State and respondents could not reopen the issue by asserting that it was a Hindu temple.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied res judicata to the issue decided in the earlier litigation and treated the prior Supreme Court judgment, State of Rajasthan v. Shri Sajjanlal Panjawat, as binding. The Court stated that the issue could not be reopened in the present proceedings.

predicates.public_trust_temple_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the character or management of a public temple trust.
predicates.same_issue_decided_in_prior_judgment: A prior judgment in litigation involving the relevant parties determined the same issue.
predicates.current_party_seeks_to_reopen_issue: A party in the later proceeding seeks a determination inconsistent with the prior decision on that issue.

issues.definition: When a public-temple proceeding involves an issue already determined in a prior judgment and a party seeks to reopen it, the issue cannot be reopened.
